title: The Travels of Ibn Battuta
intro: Ibn Battuta, a Maghrebi Muslim scholar from Tangier, set off in 1325 at the age of 21 to make the hajj to Mecca. Over thirty years he visited much of Africa, Asia and the Iberian Peninsula, and the total is put at around 117,000 km.
ending: He returned to Morocco early in 1354 and, at the suggestion of the Marinid ruler Abu Inan Faris, dictated an account of his travels to Ibn Juzayy. Modern scholars doubt that he visited every place the account describes.

stops.text: Ibn Battuta set off from his home town at the age of 21 to perform a hajj to Mecca, a journey that would ordinarily take sixteen months. He did not return to Morocco for 24 years.
stops.quote: On 2 Rajab 725 AH (14 June 1325 AD), Ibn Battuta set off from his home town at the age of 21 to perform a hajj (pilgrimage) to Mecca, a journey that would ordinarily take sixteen months.

stops.text: He arrived at the port, then part of the Bahri Mamluk empire, after a journey of over 3,500 km. There Sheikh Burhanuddin is supposed to have foretold that he would become a world traveller.
stops.quote: In the early spring of 1326, after a journey of over 3,500 km (2,200 mi), Ibn Battuta arrived at the port of Alexandria, at the time part of the Bahri Mamluk empire.

stops.text: He reached Damascus by a side trip from Cairo, a route the Mamluk authorities kept safe for pilgrims because of the holy places along it. He spent Ramadan there, in August, before joining a caravan south to Medina.
stops.quote: After spending the Muslim month of Ramadan, during August, in Damascus, he joined a caravan travelling the 1,300 km (810 mi) south to Medina, site of the Mosque of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.

stops.text: He completed his first pilgrimage and took the honorific status of El-Hajji. Rather than going home, he decided to carry on travelling, choosing the Ilkhanate, a Mongol khanate to the northeast, as his next destination.
stops.quote: upon his arrival to Mecca he completed his first pilgrimage, in November, and he took the honorific status of El-Hajji.

stops.text: After a six-month detour into Iran that took him to Isfahan and Shiraz, he arrived in Baghdad. Parts of the city were still ruined from the damage done by Hulagu Khan's army in 1258.
stops.quote: Finally, he returned across the mountains to Baghdad, arriving there in June 1327. Parts of the city were still ruined from the damage inflicted by Hulagu Khan's invading army in 1258.

legs.title: Arabia and the East African coast, c. 1329–1332

stops.text: After the hajj he went to Jeddah and followed the Red Sea coast in small boats, then through Yemen, where he met the Rasulid king at Taiz. He probably went on directly to Aden; his visit to Sanaa is doubtful.
stops.quote: In all likelihood, he went directly from Taiz to the important trading port of Aden, arriving around the beginning of 1329 or 1331.

stops.text: He sailed from Aden to Zeila and Cape Guardafui, about a week at each. At Mogadishu he found a Somali sultan, Abu Bakr ibn Shaikh 'Umar, and many rich merchants selling fine fabric abroad, including to Egypt.
stops.quote: When Ibn Battuta arrived in 1332, Mogadishu stood at the zenith of its prosperity. He described it as "an exceedingly large city" with many rich merchants

stops.text: Kilwa was an important transit centre of the gold trade. He described it as one of the finest and most beautifully built towns, with wooden buildings, and wrote favourably of its ruler, Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman.
stops.quote: Ibn Battuta recorded his visit to the Kilwa Sultanate in 1330, and commented favourably on the humility and religion of its ruler, Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman

stops.text: Having crossed to Anatolia on a Genoese ship from Latakia to Alanya, he went west to Antalya. There he met the fityan associations of young artisans, whose hospitality impressed him. His later route across Anatolia is confused in the Rihla.
stops.quote: He then journeyed westwards along the coast to the port of Antalya. In the town he met members of one of the semi-religious fityan associations.

stops.text: He joined the expedition taking Princess Bayalun home to give birth, his first journey beyond the Islamic world. He met the emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos, visited Hagia Sophia and spoke with an Orthodox priest about Jerusalem.
stops.quote: Arriving in Constantinople towards the end of 1332 (or 1334), he met the Byzantine emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos. He visited the great church of Hagia Sophia and spoke with an Eastern Orthodox priest about his travels in the city of Jerusalem.

stops.text: After a month in Constantinople he returned to Astrakhan and Sarai, then went on to Bukhara and Samarkand. He visited the Chagatai khan Tarmashirin and noted the city walls still ruined from the Mongol invasion of 1220.
stops.quote: Then he continued past the Caspian and Aral Seas to Bukhara and Samarkand, the latter of which he praised as "one of the grandest and finest cities, and the most perfect of them". Here he visited the court of another Mongol khan, Tarmashirin (r. 1331–1334) of the Chagatai Khanate.

stops.text: He crossed the Hindu Kush and reached the Indus on 12 September 1333, then went to Delhi, where Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq appointed him a qadi. For six years he alternated between favour and suspicion of treason.
stops.quote: Ibn Battuta and his party reached the Indus River on 12 September 1333. From there, he made his way to Delhi and became acquainted with the sultan, Muhammad bin Tughluq.

stops.text: Given charge of an embassy to China in 1341, he was robbed and kidnapped by bandits on the way to the coast. At Calicut he was the guest of the Zamorin, and a storm sank one of the expedition's ships.
stops.quote: While in Calicut, Battuta was the guest of the ruling Zamorin. While Ibn Battuta visited a mosque on shore, a storm arose and one of the ships of his expedition sank.

stops.text: The leaders of the recently Islamised islands gave him pearls, gold jewellery and slaves and made leaving by ship impossible. He became chief judge, married into the royal family, and resigned after his strict rulings antagonised the rulers.
stops.quote: He spent nine months on the islands, much longer than he had intended. When he arrived at the capital, Malé, Ibn Battuta did not plan to stay.

stops.text: After a 40-day voyage he was the guest of the pious sultan Al-Malik Al-Zahir Jamal-ad-Din for about two weeks. No territory east of Samudra Pasai was ruled by a Muslim, and the sultan sent him on to China.
stops.quote: In 1345, Ibn Battuta travelled to Samudra Pasai Sultanate (called "al-Jawa") in present-day Aceh, Northern Sumatra, after 40 days voyage from Sunur Kawan.

stops.text: Muslims called the city Zaitun, but he found no olives. The head of the local Muslim merchants welcomed him with flags, drums and trumpets. Some scholars have questioned whether he reached China at all, suspecting passages borrowed from other authors.
stops.quote: In the year 1345, Ibn Battuta arrived at Quanzhou in China's Fujian province, then under the rule of the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty.

stops.text: He is said to have called himself the long-lost ambassador from Delhi and to have been invited to the Yuan court. Scholars point to numerous errors in his account of China, such as confusing the Yellow River with the Grand Canal.
stops.quote: In Beijing, Ibn Battuta referred to himself as the long-lost ambassador from the Delhi Sultanate and was invited to the Yuan imperial court of Emperor Huizong

legs.title: Home by way of the Black Death, Spain and the Sahara, 1348–1354

stops.text: He arrived intending to retrace his first hajj and learned that his father had died fifteen years earlier. The Black Death had struck, and he later returned to Damascus in July, when the toll had reached 2,400 victims each day.
stops.quote: In 1348, Ibn Battuta arrived in Damascus with the intention of retracing the route of his first hajj. He then learned that his father had died 15 years earlier, and death became the dominant theme for the next year or so. The Black Death had struck, and he stopped in Homs as the plague spread through Syria, Palestine, and Arabia.

stops.text: After one last detour to Sardinia he returned to Tangier by way of Fez, nearly a quarter of a century after leaving. He found that his mother had also died a few months before.
stops.quote: On the way he made one last detour to Sardinia, then, in 1349, returned to Tangier by way of Fez, only to discover that his mother had also died a few months before.

stops.text: He joined Muslims leaving Tangier to defend Gibraltar against Alfonso XI of Castile and León. The Black Death had killed Alfonso before he arrived, so he turned the trip into a sight-seeing tour ending in Granada.
stops.quote: King Alfonso XI of Castile and León had threatened to attack Gibraltar, so in 1350, Ibn Battuta joined a group of Muslims leaving Tangier with the intention of defending the port. By the time he arrived, the Black Death had killed Alfonso and the threat of invasion had receded, so he turned the trip into a sight-seeing tour ending up in Granada.

stops.text: He left Fez and made his way to this town on the northern edge of the Sahara. There he bought a number of camels and stayed for four months before setting out with a caravan.
stops.quote: In the autumn of 1351, Ibn Battuta left Fez and made his way to the town of Sijilmasa on the northern edge of the Sahara in present-day Morocco. There he bought a number of camels and stayed for four months.

stops.text: The caravan reached the salt mines after 25 days. The local buildings were made from slabs of salt cut by the slaves of the Masufa tribe, and he recorded that the place was plagued by flies and the water was brackish.
stops.quote: He set out again with a caravan in February 1352 and, after 25 days, arrived at the dry salt lake bed of Taghaza with its salt mines.

stops.text: After meeting Mansa Suleyman at the capital of the Mali Empire, he travelled by camel to Timbuktu, at that time a small and relatively unimportant city. After a short stay he went down the Niger to Gao in a canoe.
stops.quote: He left the capital in February accompanied by a local Malian merchant and journeyed overland by camel to Timbuktu. Though in the next two centuries it would become the most important city in the region, at that time it was a small city and relatively unimportant.

stops.text: After a month in Gao, then an important commercial centre, he left with a large caravan. A message from the Sultan of Morocco ordered him home, and he set off for Sijilmasa in September 1353.
stops.quote: After spending a month in Gao, Ibn Battuta set off with a large caravan for the oasis of Takedda. On his journey across the desert, he received a message from the Sultan of Morocco commanding him to return home. He set off for Sijilmasa in September 1353, accompanying a large caravan transporting 600 female slaves, and arrived back in Morocco early in 1354.

notes: 24 stops. Many places in the article are only passed over (Tunis, Cairo, Isfahan, Shiraz, Tabriz, Mosul, Zeila, Mombasa, Bolghar, Sylhet, Chittagong, Sri Lanka, Hangzhou, Oualata, the Mali capital) and were left out to stay within 24. Article doubts: Sanaa (doubtful), the Volga trip to Bolghar (very unlikely), the Anatolian itinerary (confused), China (some scholars question it), the Maldives conversion story. Dating is inconsistent in the article: Mecca stay 1327-1330 or after the 1328 hajj; Aden 1329 or 1331; Kilwa 1330 but Mogadishu 1332 (the stops follow the article's order, so Kilwa's year is earlier than Mogadishu's); Anatolia 1330 or 1332; Constantinople 1332 or 1334. Years not given in the article and set by me from its sequence: Samarkand 1333 (Tarmashirin's reign 1331-1334), Calicut and Malé 1341 (the embassy year; the Maldives stay falls between 1341 and 1345), Beijing 1345, Timbuktu 1353 (inferred from the Taghaza date of February 1352 and Gao in September 1353). Beijing is given by land, though the article also mentions the Grand Canal by boat. Gao is given 'sea' because the article says he went by canoe down the Niger. 'Damascus' by land and Tangier by sea are my reading of the article's brief account. Wikipedia titles: Constantinople stop uses 'Istanbul', Calicut uses 'Kozhikode'. Entry 'tunisia' not used (Tunis dropped). 'aden' entry is the city.
